q.q: Which statement best describes the waterfall model?
o: The system is developed as a series of evolving prototypes
Each stage is completed and signed off before the next begins
Users review a working version at the end of every fortnight
Stages overlap so that coding starts during analysis
q.why: Waterfall is strictly sequential, with sign-off at the end of each stage.

q.q: In the waterfall model, what is a deliverable?
o: A list of risks identified for the project at the start
The end product of a stage that becomes the input to the next stage
A payment made by the client at the end of each stage
The finished system handed to the client at the very end
q.why: Every waterfall stage produces a deliverable, such as the system specification, that the next builds on.

q.q: A waterfall project discovers during testing that a requirement was misunderstood. What must happen?
o: The project returns to an earlier stage and later stages are repeated
The fault is simply fixed in the next two-week sprint
Nothing, because testing only checks that the code runs
The maintenance team fixes it after installation, without changing documents
q.why: Going back up the waterfall is possible but costly.

q.q: What is a development methodology?
o: An agreed framework of stages, roles and documents that structures development
A programming language and set of tools chosen for building the system
A single test plan used by testers to check the finished system
A prioritised list of user requirements agreed with the client
q.why: No single methodology is best for every project.

q.q: Which list gives the stages of the waterfall model in the order given in the notes?
o: Requirements, design, testing, implementation, maintenance
Requirements, design, implementation, testing, maintenance
Requirements, implementation, design, testing, maintenance
Design, requirements, implementation, maintenance, testing
q.why: Work moves down a fixed sequence of five stages.

q.q: When does the waterfall model work best?
o: When requirements are stable and well understood at the outset
When a working version is needed within two weeks
When requirements are unclear and likely to change often
When users must shape the system as it is developed
q.why: So much depends on getting the first stage right.

q.q: Why does sign-off at the end of each waterfall stage help the client and developer?
o: It removes the need to produce any documentation
It allows stages to overlap so the project finishes sooner
Progress is easy to measure and work can be invoiced stage by stage
It means users can change requirements at any time
q.why: Sign-off marks the end of each stage.

q.q: Compared with an iterative approach, when is working software seen in the waterfall model?
o: Early, after the first iteration
At the end of every sprint
Only near the end, after testing
After each prototype is built
q.why: Iterative approaches show working software early.

q.q: A pupil answers 'describe the main features of the waterfall model' only by naming its five stages. How much credit is this likely to earn?
o: No credit at all
Five points
Full marks
Only one point
q.why: Naming the stages on its own counts as only one point.

q.q: What is the deliverable of the design stage of the waterfall model?
o: The design document
The user manual
The system specification
The test plan results
q.why: Design turns the specification into a design document from which programmers code.

q.q: In the waterfall model described in this topic, which stage includes migrating data from the old system?
o: Design
Testing
Analysis
Maintenance
q.why: In this textbook's version of the model, installation and data migration fall under maintenance.

q.q: Why must the system specification be complete?
o: So that programmers can skip unit testing
So that the whole project can be invoiced in advance
Missing requirements are difficult and expensive to add later
Because users will never be consulted again at all
q.why: In a sequential model, adding a requirement late means going back through several stages.

q.q: If a system is completely new, what becomes the main source of information at the requirements stage?
o: Observation of the existing system in use
The design document from a previous project
Documents sampled from the current system
The users' own descriptions of their needs
q.why: With no existing system to investigate, users' descriptions are the main evidence.

q.q: What is the deliverable of the implementation stage in the waterfall model?
o: An accepted system
The design document
The system specification
Unit-tested program code
q.why: Programmers write code from the design and unit test their modules.

q.q: How should the testing stage of the waterfall model be described for full marks?
o: Programmers testing their own modules as they write each section of code
Checked against the system specification using a test plan, so requirements were not misunderstood
Users suggesting changes as each new screen is shown to them during the build
Checking that the program works properly and does not crash when it is run
q.why: The notes warn against describing testing as just 'checking the program works'.

q.q: Why must the design document be precise?
o: It replaces the test plan
Programmers code directly from it
Users sign it off at acceptance
It is sent to external beta testers
q.why: The design document is the programmers' input.

q.q: Which of these is done during the design stage of the waterfall model?
o: Interviewing users about the current system's problems
Dividing the software into units and defining how they interact
Migrating existing data and supporting users
Writing code for the modules allocated to each programmer
q.why: Design also covers processes, inputs/outputs, the interface and hardware.

q.q: Why does some testing happen inside the implementation stage?
o: Beta testers try each module as soon as it is finished
The test plan is written during implementation
Programmers unit test their own modules as they go
Users carry out acceptance testing while code is written
q.why: Unit testing is part of implementation.

q.q: Which people mainly carry out the testing stage of the waterfall model?
o: Support and maintenance staff
Testers, then users
The systems analyst only
Programmers only
q.why: Testers check against the specification; users then carry out acceptance testing.

q.q: At which two stages of the waterfall model are users mainly involved?
o: Implementation and maintenance
Design and testing
Analysis and testing
Design and implementation
q.why: Users supply requirements during analysis and accept the system during testing.

q.q: Why is user input especially important when there is no existing system?
o: The new system will not need any acceptance testing by its users
There is nothing to observe, so users' descriptions are the main source of requirements
The waterfall model then becomes an iterative model with prototypes
Users must write some of the program code themselves, as no analyst can
q.why: With no current system, the analyst depends on what users say they need.

q.q: What is the main consequence of limited user involvement in the waterfall model?
o: The documentation produced at each stage is always poor and incomplete
Misunderstandings may stay hidden until testing, when they are costly to fix
The project always finishes earlier than planned, as users cause no delays
Users have to learn to program so they can check the system themselves
q.why: No working software is seen until late, so errors introduced at handovers travel a long way.

q.q: Why can misunderstandings arise at each handover in a waterfall project?
o: Testers change the requirements before any coding has started
Users write each handover document themselves without the analyst
Each group interprets the previous group's document, not what users actually said
Programmers are not given any design document to work from
q.why: Analyst, designers and programmers each interpret the previous document.

q.q: How does formal sign-off of each deliverable reduce risk in a waterfall project?
o: Users no longer need to do acceptance testing
Requirements can then be changed freely later
Testing can begin before design is complete
Everyone agrees what was intended before work moves on
q.why: Sign-off ensures agreement at each stage.

q.q: Which good practice ensures agreed changes are recorded and their knock-on effects managed?
o: Change control
Timeboxing
Daily Scrum
Pair programming
q.why: Change control manages changes in a waterfall project.

q.q: Why should the test plan be written from the specification?
o: So testing checks every requirement, not just whether the code runs
So programmers can test their own code only
So users do not need to be consulted during analysis
So the design document can be skipped
q.why: A test plan from the specification covers each requirement.

q.q: Which is an advantage of the waterfall model?
o: Each stage has a clear deliverable, so progress is easy to measure
Requirements can change freely at any time
It needs no documentation to be produced
Users see working software after only two weeks
q.why: Defined deliverables and sign-off make progress measurable.

q.q: Why can a misunderstanding be so costly in a waterfall project?
o: There is no maintenance stage in the waterfall model
Programmers do not work from any design document
The client cannot be invoiced for any of the work done
It may pass through several stages before testing finds it
q.why: Errors introduced at a handover are often found only at testing.

q.q: For which project is the waterfall model most suitable?
o: A council system implementing a fixed, published fee structure
A charity website whose content changes every week
A research prototype exploring untested AI ideas
A games start-up unsure which features players will like
q.why: Stable, well-defined requirements suit the sequential model.

q.q: Why does the waterfall model suit fixed-price contracts?
o: With stable requirements, cost and timescale can be predicted with some confidence
Risk analysis is carried out in every loop of the project
Working software is delivered to the client after each sprint
Users can add new features at any time without any extra charge
q.why: Easier estimation is an advantage when requirements are stable.

q.q: How does the waterfall model use specialist staff efficiently?
o: Specialists can be moved between stages to balance workloads easily
Specialists are not needed because users write the code
All staff are multi-skilled and work on every stage together
Specialists can move to the same stage of another project once theirs is signed off
q.why: Moving staff between stages is harder; multi-skilled teams are an Agile feature.

q.q: Which explains the 'inflexible' weakness of the waterfall model in the way that scores most?
o: The waterfall model is inflexible, which is a disadvantage for the client and for developers
Waterfall is inflexible because it is a very old model that dates from the 1970s
The waterfall model is not flexible enough for many projects in the modern world
If needs change after design is signed off, the project must return to design, adding cost and delay
q.why: Explaining the consequence earns more than naming the weakness.

q.q: Which project would NOT suit the waterfall model?
o: Updating payroll to new HMRC rules
A new mobile app for a start-up
A system defined by regulation
A safety system needing formal sign-off
q.why: Unclear or changing requirements do not suit waterfall.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of the waterfall model?
o: No part of the system can be used until near the end
Little documentation is produced
Progress is hard to measure between stages
Cost is impossible to estimate with stable requirements
q.why: Late delivery of anything useful is a weakness.

q.q: What is the distinguishing feature of the spiral model?
o: Each stage is completed once only
Risk analysis takes place in every loop
It has no testing stage at all
Users are only involved at the end
q.why: Boehm's spiral model is risk-driven.

q.q: What does each iteration in iterative development produce?
o: A complete, final system ready for sign-off
A working version that users can review
Only a design document for the next stage
A burn down chart of the work remaining
q.why: Each cycle produces a version whose feedback shapes the next.

q.q: For which project would the spiral model be most appropriate?
o: A five-page website for a local café
Changing the font on an existing app
A spreadsheet for a school tuck shop
A new air-traffic control system using untried technology
q.why: Large, novel, high-risk projects justify the cost of risk analysis.

q.q: Who proposed the spiral model, and when?
o: Kent Beck, in the late 1990s
James Martin, in 1991
Barry Boehm, in 1968
Barry Boehm, in 1986
q.why: James Martin popularised RAD; Kent Beck developed XP.

q.q: Which is the correct order of the four quadrants in each spiral loop?
o: Objectives, risk analysis, develop and test, review and plan
Risk analysis, objectives, review and plan, develop and test
Develop and test, objectives, risk analysis, review and plan
Objectives, develop and test, risk analysis, review and plan
q.why: Each loop sets objectives, resolves risks, builds and tests, then reviews.

q.q: In the spiral model, how are risks often resolved in the second quadrant?
o: By dropping low-priority features
By holding a daily Scrum meeting
By building a prototype or running a simulation
By signing off the design document
q.why: Prototypes or simulations test uncertain ideas.

q.q: Which is a drawback of iterative development?
o: It suits only projects whose requirements are completely fixed
Misunderstandings are only found at the very end of the project
It needs regular user availability and control to stop scope growing
Nothing useful can be delivered before the whole project ends
q.why: Iterative development finds misunderstandings early, but has these costs.

q.q: Why is the spiral model overkill for a small, low-risk project?
o: It has no testing, so quality suffers
Risk analysis needs expertise and costs money
It requires all requirements to be fixed first
It cannot produce any working software
q.why: The overhead of risk analysis is high.

q.q: A pupil describes the spiral model as 'going round in circles until the system is finished'. What key point is missing?
o: Timeboxing: fixing the deadline for each build
Risk analysis: identifying and resolving risks in each loop
Sign-off: approving each stage before the next
Refactoring: tidying code without changing it
q.why: Without risk analysis the answer usually misses the key mark.

q.q: What happens to a throwaway prototype?
o: It is refined until it becomes the final system
It is kept as a backup of the live system
It is sold to the client as a finished product
It is discarded once the requirements have been agreed
q.why: Its job is to clarify requirements; the real system is then built properly.

q.q: Which is a risk of evolutionary prototyping?
o: Rushed early design decisions may remain in the final system
Users never see a working version of the system
Requirements must be completely fixed before it starts
None of the effort put into the prototype is used
q.why: Poor early structure can make the final system harder to maintain.

q.q: Why are prototypes useful in analysis?
o: They remove the need for a project manager on the team
They guarantee a lower price for the whole project
Users can react to real screens and clarify requirements they find hard to describe
They replace the need to test the finished system against a plan
q.why: Seeing and using a model helps users say what they actually need.

q.q: Is prototyping a methodology in its own right?
o: No, it is a technique used inside methodologies such as RAD, Agile and spiral
Yes, it is a full methodology that replaces the waterfall model for all projects
No, it is a type of acceptance testing done after implementation
Yes, it is simply another name for Rapid Application Development
q.why: The notes describe prototyping as a technique, not a methodology.

q.q: What is an evolutionary prototype?
o: A paper sketch of each screen with navigation arrows
A prototype used only to test hardware speed
A prototype discarded once requirements are agreed
A prototype refined repeatedly until it becomes the final system
q.why: Evolutionary prototypes become the product.

q.q: Which tools are typically used for a throwaway prototype?
o: Quick mock-up tools such as a slide or wireframing app
Automated tests written before the code
The production language and tools from the start
The live system's database and full test suite
q.why: Throwaway prototypes do not need production quality.

q.q: What is the main benefit of throwaway prototyping?
o: Users receive a working system sooner
No effort at all is wasted on the prototype
The final system is built cleanly to a proper design
The prototype is delivered as the product
q.why: Those other benefits belong to evolutionary prototyping.

q.q: A pupil writes that a throwaway prototype 'is thrown away because it failed'. Why is this wrong?
o: It is discarded only if users reject the design
It is discarded by design, once it has clarified the requirements
It is never discarded; it becomes the final system
It is kept and sold to other clients later
q.why: Discarding it is planned, not a sign of failure.

q.q: Why are users who try prototypes more likely to accept the final system?
o: They no longer need any training
They never see any errors in it
They have written its program code
They feel involved in its development
q.why: Involvement increases acceptance.

q.q: What happens in RAD if time runs short?
o: The deadline is extended
Testing is skipped
The project restarts
Low-priority requirements are dropped
q.why: Requirements are prioritised and the timebox is fixed.

q.q: Which is the final phase of RAD?
o: Cutover
Maintenance
User design
Construction
q.why: Cutover is the transition from the old system to the new one.

q.q: How are users involved in RAD?
o: Continually, through frequent prototypes
Not at all, to save time
Only at the very start
Only at acceptance testing
q.why: Users give feedback on prototypes throughout user design and construction.

q.q: What is timeboxing?
o: Holding a 15-minute meeting at the same time each day
Setting a strict timescale that must not be overrun
Planning the number of loops in a spiral project
Recording the time each programmer spends on a task
q.why: Timeboxing fixes the deadline; features are dropped instead.

q.q: Who popularised RAD, and in which year was his book published?
o: James Martin, 1968
James Martin, 1991
Kent Beck, 1999
Barry Boehm, 1986
q.why: Martin's 1991 book set out the method.

q.q: Which is the correct order of the four RAD phases?
o: Requirements planning, construction, user design, cutover
Construction, user design, requirements planning, cutover
Requirements planning, user design, construction, cutover
User design, requirements planning, cutover, construction
q.why: User design and construction often loop several times.

q.q: In which RAD phase do analysts and users work together using prototypes to design functions and compare interfaces?
o: User design
Construction
Cutover
Requirements planning
q.why: User involvement is most intensive in user design.

q.q: In which RAD phase do data conversion, changeover and training take place?
o: Construction
User design
Cutover
Requirements planning
q.why: Cutover replaces the old system with the new.

q.q: Why do requirements not need to be fully fixed in RAD requirements planning?
o: Programmers decide the requirements later
Requirements are fixed by the timebox instead
Changes are expected as users see prototypes
RAD projects do not have any requirements
q.why: RAD expects requirements to change through feedback.

q.q: What is the product backlog?
o: A prioritised wish list of everything the product should do
A list of bugs found in testing
The features chosen for the current sprint only
The Scrum master's diary of meetings
q.why: Items move from the product backlog into the release backlog.

q.q: Who acts as the voice of the client in a Scrum team?
o: The systems analyst
The Scrum master
The product owner
A tester
q.why: The product owner sets priorities in the backlogs on the client's behalf.

q.q: What is the purpose of a sprint retrospective?
o: To write the product backlog for the next release
To reflect on and improve the team's way of working
To show the finished product to the client
To sign off the design document
q.why: The retrospective looks at how the team worked; the review looks at the product.

q.q: What is the purpose of a sprint review?
o: To agree the daily tasks for each developer
To examine the finished work and show it to the product owner
To write the initial product backlog
To reflect on how the team worked together
q.why: The review is about the product built.

q.q: What is the release backlog?
o: Features chosen from the product backlog for the next release, broken into work items
A list of every feature the product should eventually do, in priority order
A chart of the work remaining in a sprint against the days
The list of bugs reported by users after the product is released
q.why: Release planning moves features from the product backlog into the release backlog.

q.q: What is the role of the Scrum master?
o: To approve each stage's deliverable before the next stage begins
To make sure the team works effectively, arranging meetings and removing obstacles
To write all the program code for each sprint increment
To represent the client, own the backlogs and set the priorities
q.why: The Scrum master serves the team; the product owner represents the client.

q.q: Why can a Scrum team move someone onto a task that is overrunning?
o: Members are all specialists
The product owner codes it
The timebox is extended
Members are multi-skilled
q.why: Multi-skilled teams are flexible.

q.q: In what year was the Manifesto for Agile Software Development published?
q.why: 1986 is Boehm's spiral, 1991 Martin's RAD book, 1968 the NATO conference.

q.q: 'As a member, I want to renew online so that I don't have to queue.' What is this?
o: A burn down chart entry
A sprint retrospective action
A user story in the product backlog
A daily Scrum question
q.why: Product backlog items are often written as user stories.

q.q: Which is NOT one of the three daily Scrum questions?
o: What did I do yesterday?
What will I do today?
How much will the project cost?
What obstacles are in my way?
q.why: The daily Scrum focuses on progress and obstacles, not budgets.

q.q: On a burn down chart, the actual line is above the ideal line. What does this mean?
o: The backlog is now empty
The team is ahead of schedule
The team is behind schedule
The sprint has finished early
q.why: More work remains than planned.

q.q: A 15-day sprint starts with 90 hours of work. What is the ideal work remaining after day 5?
o: 45 hours
30 hours
75 hours
60 hours
q.why: Ideal rate = 90 ÷ 15 = 6 hours per day; 90 − 6 × 5 = 60 hours.

q.q: A 10-day sprint has 60 story points. On day 4, 42 points remain against an ideal of 36. What does this show?
o: The team is exactly on schedule
The team is 18 points behind schedule
The team is 6 points behind schedule
The team is 6 points ahead of schedule
q.why: 42 – 36 = 6 more points remain than planned, so the team is behind.

q.q: In the same 10-day sprint of 60 points, what is the ideal rate at which work should be completed?
o: 12 points per day
10 points per day
6 points per day
4 points per day
q.why: 60 ÷ 10 = 6 points per day.

q.q: On a burn down chart, the actual line is flat for two days. What does this most likely mean?
o: No work was completed, often because of an obstacle
New items were added to the sprint
The team was ahead of schedule
The team finished all the work early
q.why: A flat section means no work remaining was reduced.

q.q: How long does a daily Scrum usually last?
o: About 1 hour
About 5 minutes
About half a day
About 15 minutes
q.why: It is short and often held standing up.

q.q: Who takes responsibility for resolving obstacles raised at the daily Scrum?
o: Each developer alone
The Scrum master
The client
The product owner
q.why: Anyone can contribute ideas, but the Scrum master is responsible.

q.q: What does a burn down chart plot?
o: Features delivered against the number of releases
Work completed against the cost of the sprint
Work remaining against the days of the sprint
Number of bugs against the number of testers
q.why: The ideal line falls straight from all the work to none.

q.q: What is the main benefit of the daily Scrum?
o: Problems are spotted within a day rather than at the end of the sprint
The client can formally sign off each day's work at the meeting
The whole product backlog is rewritten from scratch every day
Developers no longer need to write any automated tests at all
q.why: Close daily monitoring stops the project drifting.

q.q: In test-driven development, what is written first?
o: The design document
The program code
The user manual
An automated test
q.why: TDD writes a failing test first, then the code to make it pass.

q.q: Which is a benefit of pair programming?
o: It removes the need for any other testing
It lets one programmer work faster on their own
Errors are spotted immediately and knowledge is shared
It halves the number of computers that must be bought
q.why: The navigator reviews code as it is written.

q.q: What is refactoring?
o: Improving code structure without changing what it does
Rewriting the requirements after each release
Adding new features to the code as quickly as possible
Merging every programmer's code into one version
q.why: Refactoring keeps behaviour the same while making the code cleaner.

q.q: In pair programming, what does the 'navigator' do?
o: Represents the client's wishes
Types the code at the keyboard
Writes the user documentation
Reviews each line and thinks ahead
q.why: The driver types; the navigator reviews; they swap regularly.

q.q: Who developed extreme programming, and when?
o: James Martin, in 1991
Kent Beck, in the early 1970s
Barry Boehm, in 1986
Kent Beck, in the late 1990s
q.why: XP was developed by Kent Beck in the late 1990s.

q.q: How does XP differ in focus from Scrum?
o: XP is a sequential model; Scrum is an iterative model
XP concentrates on how code is written; Scrum on how the project is organised
XP needs no customer involvement; Scrum needs a product owner
XP concentrates on how the project is organised; Scrum on how code is written
q.why: Many teams combine XP practices with Scrum sprints.

q.q: What is continuous integration?
o: Two programmers sharing a single workstation and swapping roles
Releasing working software to customers every few weeks
Merging code into the shared version several times a day with automatic tests
Writing a failing automated test before writing any of the code
q.why: Integration problems are found within hours, not at the end.

q.q: What is the correct order of the TDD cycle?
o: Write the code, write a test, release the code
Write the code, tidy it, then write a passing test
Tidy the code, write a test, write the code
Write a failing test, write just enough code to pass, tidy the code
q.why: The test fails first, just enough code passes it, then the code is refactored.

q.q: Which is a drawback of XP?
o: Feedback from customers is very slow
It needs a committed customer available throughout
Knowledge stays with one programmer
Defects are only found at the end
q.why: XP relies on an on-site customer.

q.q: Why does an on-site customer help an XP team?
o: Requirements are clarified at once, not weeks later
The customer writes the automated tests
The customer pairs with each programmer
The customer replaces the Scrum master
q.why: The customer representative answers questions immediately.

q.q: Requirements for a new system are unclear and the client can meet the team daily. Which approach is most suitable?
o: No approach; the project should not start
Waterfall with a longer analysis stage
Agile
Waterfall
q.why: Agile welcomes change and relies on regular customer contact.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of Agile?
o: It cannot respond to changing requirements
Users see nothing until the very end
The accuracy of time estimates depends heavily on the Scrum master
It has no way of prioritising work
q.why: Estimating is hard and relies on the Scrum master's experience.

q.q: Which approach protects a fixed deadline by dropping low-priority features?
o: Extreme programming
RAD
Waterfall
Spiral
q.why: RAD timeboxes the project and sacrifices desirable add-ons.

q.q: Which approach has a team of specialists for each stage?
o: Extreme programming
RAD
Agile
Waterfall
q.why: Agile uses a small multi-skilled team.

q.q: In which approach is the first working version usually delivered after the first sprint?
o: Spiral
RAD
Waterfall
Agile
q.why: Waterfall delivers near the end; RAD gives early prototypes within the timebox.

q.q: Why is a fixed price and scope hard to agree for an Agile project?
o: Agile teams are made up of separate specialists for each stage
Agile requires all requirements to be fixed and signed off first
Agile projects never produce any working software until the very end
Requirements are expected to change and the customer commits time throughout
q.why: The backlog is reprioritised each sprint, so scope is flexible.

q.q: Which approach produces the most thorough documentation?
o: Waterfall
Agile
Extreme programming
RAD
q.why: RAD and Agile produce lighter documentation.

q.q: Which is a main weakness of RAD in the comparison framework?
o: It has no prioritisation of requirements
It produces no prototypes for users
It is inflexible and discovers errors late
It needs committed users and skilled staff and can be costly
q.why: Inflexibility and late error discovery are waterfall weaknesses.

q.q: What should an extended answer recommending a methodology always do?
o: Compare all three approaches against the scenario and give a justified recommendation
Describe only the chosen approach in as much detail as possible
Give the advantages of Agile because it is the newest approach
List the features of each approach without linking them to the scenario
q.why: Generic lists with no link to the context score poorly.

q.q: A medical device must meet strict regulations, needs full documentation and has stable requirements. Which approach best fits?
o: Agile
Evolutionary prototyping
Waterfall
RAD
q.why: Stable requirements and the need for documentation and formal sign-off suit waterfall.
